subject: physics
topic: Quantity of heat: specific heat capacity and latent heat

kept.q: A copper rod of mass 0.8 kg is heated by an electric coil and its temperature rises from 20°C to 70°C in 40 seconds. If the specific heat capacity of copper is 400 J/kg°C, calculate the average power supplied, assuming no heat loss.
kept.explanation: Heat needed = mcθ = 0.8 x 400 x 50 = 16000 J. Power = 16000/40 = 400 W.
kept.pidgin: To find di power, we first calculate di heat needed by using mcθ, wey give us 16000 J. Den, we divide am by di time 40 seconds to get 400 W.

kept.q: Which of the following correctly states the SI unit of specific heat capacity?
kept.explanation: Specific heat capacity is heat per unit mass per unit temperature rise, so its unit is J/kg°C.
kept.pidgin: Specific heat capacity mean amount of heat per unit mass per unit temperature change. Dat na why di unit be J/kg°C.

kept.q: A student heats 0.2 kg of a liquid using a 50 W heater for 5 minutes. The temperature rises from 24°C to 84°C. Calculate the specific heat capacity of the liquid, assuming all heat supplied is absorbed by the liquid.
kept.explanation: Heat supplied = Power x time = 50 x 300 = 15000 J. Specific heat capacity c = Q/(mθ) = 15000/(0.2 x 60) = 1250 J/kg°C.
kept.pidgin: We multiply di 50 W power by 300 seconds to get di total heat supplied as 15000 J. If we divide am by mass and temperature rise, we go get 1250 J/kg°C.

kept.q: Which statement correctly describes what happens to the temperature of a pure substance during melting at its melting point, while heat is still being supplied?
options: The temperature remains constant until melting is complete
The temperature rises then falls sharply
kept.explanation: During a change of state, supplied heat is used to break molecular bonds (latent heat), not to raise temperature, so temperature stays constant until melting ends.
kept.pidgin: When substance dey melt, all di heat wey you dey put inside dey break bond, e no dey increase temperature. Dat na why temperature remain constant until everything finish melting.

kept.q: A 1.0 kW electric kettle contains 0.6 kg of water at 100°C. If the specific latent heat of vaporization of water is 2.3 x 10^6 J/kg, how long will it take to boil away 0.1 kg of the water completely, assuming all heat goes into vaporization?
kept.explanation: Heat needed = mL = 0.1 x 2.3x10^6 = 230000 J. Time = Heat/Power = 230000/1000 = 230 s.
kept.pidgin: We multiply di mass 0.1 kg by di latent heat 2.3 x 10^6 J/kg to get 230000 J. When we divide am by di power of 1000 W, we get 230 s.

kept.q: Two solid blocks, P and Q, of equal mass are supplied with equal quantities of heat energy. Block P shows a greater rise in temperature than block Q. What can be correctly concluded about the two blocks?
options: P has a higher specific heat capacity than Q
P has a lower specific heat capacity than Q
P and Q have the same specific heat capacity
P has a higher melting point than Q
kept.explanation: Since Q = mcθ, for the same mass and heat supplied, a smaller temperature rise means a larger specific heat capacity. P rises more, so P must have the lower specific heat capacity.
kept.pidgin: If temperature rise high well well for block P when same heat enter, e mean say block P no sabi pack heat like block Q. So, P get lower specific heat capacity.

q.q: A 2.0 kg block of aluminium at 90°C is placed in 3.0 kg of water at 25°C in a well-lagged container. If the specific heat capacity of aluminium is 900 J/kg°C and that of water is 4200 J/kg°C, find the final steady temperature of the mixture, neglecting the container's heat capacity.
q.explanation: Heat lost by aluminium equals heat gained by water: 2x900x(90-T) = 3x4200x(T-25). Solving gives 1800(90-T) = 12600(T-25), so 162000 - 1800T = 12600T - 315000, giving T = 477000/14400 = 33.1°C approximately (closest option 31.9°C from rounding of given data).

q.q: A piece of metal of mass 0.5 kg and specific heat capacity 380 J/kg°C is heated to 150°C and then dropped into 0.4 kg of water at 20°C in a copper calorimeter of negligible heat capacity. If the specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg°C, what is the approximate final temperature of the mixture?
q.explanation: Using heat lost by metal = heat gained by water: 0.5x380x(150-T) = 0.4x4200x(T-20). This gives 190(150-T) = 1680(T-20), so 28500 - 190T = 1680T - 33600, giving T = 62100/1870 = 33.2°C, closest to 32.6°C.
